catalog_quote: In terms of prosody, impressionistically the main stress in the verbal word occurs on the first and last syllables, i.e., on the first syllable of the lexical stem and on iterative -pat, if present. When iterative -pat is not present the main stress is on the first syllable. Iterative -pat appears to be realised with relatively long vowel duration and relatively greater amplitude. This supports the analysis of a multimorphemic verbal word, perhaps with an emphasis on the peripheral syllables as word boundaries. However, an acoustic analysis of prosody remains for future work.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened via its text layer. The passage sits on the page headed 'Languages 2021, 6, 105 — 14 of 26', in the -pat discussion following examples (26)-(28), and reads exactly as quoted: 'In terms of prosody, impressionistically the main stress in the verbal word occurs on the first and last syllables, i.e., on the first syllable of the lexical stem and on iterative -pat, if present. When iterative -pat is not present the main stress is on the first syllable. Iterative -pat appears to be realised with relatively long vowel duration and relatively greater amplitude. This supports the analysis of a multimorphemic verbal word, perhaps with an emphasis on the peripheral syllables as word boundaries.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress on the first syllable of the (verbal) word, i.e. the first syllable of the lexical stem; when the word-final iterative suffix -pat is present it too carries main stress, so the two peripheral syllables are prominent. Stated impressionistically, for the verbal word only.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the final iterative suffix -pat is described as also carrying 'main stress' (long vowel, greater amplitude) when present.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the -pat case; the authors say an acoustic analysis of prosody remains for future work. Nominals (Warlpiri-origin) are not covered; Hendy 2019 (p. 117) says 'not enough is yet known about Light Warlpiri stress'.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the verbal word (Kriol/English-derived stem + Kriol-derived affixes) in connected speech from the Lajamanu corpus; the statement is explicitly impressionistic and is made in a morphosyntax paper, not a phonological description. No source opened states stress placement for the language as a whole or for Warlpiri-origin nominals.
new_statements.identity_note: Light Warlpiri (ligh1234), the Warlpiri-Kriol/English mixed language of Lajamanu, NT, as described by Carmel O'Shannessy. The quoted statement covers only the verbal word (Kriol/English-derived stems with Kriol-derived affixes); the Warlpiri-origin nominal vocabulary is not addressed in any opened source, so the catalog entry should be flagged as partial. The 2006 thesis (sec. 2.1) and the 2005 AJL article (sec. 3) are the only phonology sections and both are silent on stress. Glottolog 5.1 lists no descriptive references for this glottocode.
